scenes.visual: cell full of shredder enzymes; zymogen answer
scenes.narration: Here is the central puzzle of digestion. Your digestive enzymes are powerful enough to tear proteins apart, yet the cells that make them are themselves built from protein. So how do you manufacture a molecular shredder without shredding the factory? The answer is the zymogen, an inactive precursor. The cell builds the enzyme in a folded-but-dormant form, ships it out, and normally switches it on where digestion should happen. This single design principle, activation only where and when needed, recurs everywhere in physiology from blood clotting to apoptosis. Keep it in mind as our organizing idea.

scenes.narration: Notice that digestion is really one chemical trick repeated three times. Hydrolysis means breaking a bond by inserting water. Proteases attack the peptide bond, disaccharidases attack the glycosidic bond, and lipases attack the ester bond. In every case, water donates a hydrogen to one fragment and a hydroxyl to the other, capping both freshly broken ends. The substrates look different, the enzymes are different, but the logic is identical. If you understand one row, you understand all three. That bottom summary is the takeaway worth memorizing. Water provides the H and the OH that finish off each broken bond.

scenes.narration: This is the activation map for the digestive proteases. In the stomach, low pH converts pepsinogen into active pepsin. In the small intestine, the pancreas delivers a whole family of zymogens. Watch what trypsin does once it is switched on. It activates chymotrypsinogen, the procarboxypeptidases, and proelastase. Trypsin is the master switch. That single arrow pattern, one activated enzyme turning on all the others, is why the note at the bottom matters. It also previews a clinical point. Knock out the ability to make trypsin and the entire downstream cascade never fires, no matter how much of the other zymogens you have.

scenes.narration: Put the cascade idea to the test. On the left is the normal activation tree. Enteropeptidase switches on trypsin, and trypsin then activates chymotrypsin, the carboxypeptidases, elastase, and procolipase, a lipase helper that works even uncut. On the right, remove the ability to make trypsinogen. Now the master switch is gone, and the downstream protease zymogens stay locked, no matter how abundant they are. That is why a trypsinogen deficiency is so much worse than losing any single other zymogen. Lose one branch and you lose one enzyme. Lose trypsin, and pancreatic protein digestion collapses at once, while fat digestion is largely spared.
